Fit a regression with a network metric

Source: R/bison_brm.R
bison_brm.Rd

Fits a Bayesian regression with the brms package in which a network metric, such as node strength or edge weight, is a response or predictor. The uncertainty in the metric, estimated by the edge model, is carried into the regression by multiple imputation. Use it after bison_model() to test hypotheses about edges, nodes or whole networks, for example whether age predicts node strength.

Usage

bison_brm(
  formula,
  edgemodel_list,
  data_list,
  num_draws = 100,
  z_score = FALSE,
  cores = 4,
  chains = 2,
  scale = c("none", "centre", "z"),
  subset = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

A brms formula containing one bison() term (see Details).

edgemodel_list

A fitted bison_model object, or a list of them for an analysis of several networks.

data_list

A data frame of regression variables, or a list of data frames with one per edge model, in the same order. For edge and node metrics, each row refers to a dyad or node, and the columns named in the bison() term must hold node names that match the edge model. For global metrics, give one data frame with one row per edge model.

num_draws

Number of posterior draws of the network metric to use, which is the number of regressions fitted. 100 is a reasonable value for a final analysis; smaller values (such as 5 or 10) are useful while developing a model.

z_score

If TRUE, standardise the network variable within each posterior draw. Equivalent to scale = "z".

cores

Number of processor cores to use.

chains

Number of MCMC chains to run for each regression. MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo) draws samples from the posterior; a chain is one independent run of the sampler.

scale

How to transform the network variable within each posterior draw: "none" (default), "centre" (subtract the mean) or "z" (subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation). For edge and node metrics, transformations are applied across the rows used in the model, separately for each network, which removes differences in the average level between networks; use "none" to compare levels between networks. Global metrics have one value per network, so they are transformed across the networks.

subset

An optional logical expression, evaluated in each data frame, selecting the rows to use, e.g. subset = sex == "F". Network metrics are still calculated from the whole network; only the rows of the regression are selected. Not available for global metrics.

...

Additional arguments passed to brms::brm_multiple(), such as family or prior.

Value

A fitted brms model (a brmsfit object) combining the fits to all imputed datasets. Use summary(), brms::conditional_effects() or brms::hypothesis() on it as for any brms model.

Details

The network metric is written in the formula as a bison() term containing the metric and the data columns that identify its targets:

  • bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) for dyadic regression;

  • bison(node_strength(node_id)), bison(node_degree[0.2](node_id)) and so on for nodal regression;

  • bison(global_cv(bison_network)) and so on for global metrics, with one row of data per network.

The bison() term can be on either side of the formula, and the rest of the formula uses ordinary brms syntax, including random effects such as (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)). In the fitted model, the network variable is named after the metric, such as bison_node_strength. See extract_metric() for the metrics available.

Multiple imputation repeats an analysis on several plausible versions of the data and combines the results. Here, each version uses one posterior draw of the network metric (see bison_mice()). brms::brm_multiple() fits the regression to each version and combines the posterior draws of all the fits, so num_draws regressions are fitted and fitting time grows with num_draws. Models are fitted with the cmdstanr backend unless backend is given in ....

Edge weights are used on the link scale (log-odds for binary models, log rates for count models). Node and global metrics are calculated from edge weights on the natural scale.

With a list of edge models, a factor bison_network is added to the data, giving the position of each edge model in the list. It can be used as a predictor or random effect to compare networks.

See also

bison_brm_get_prior() to see and set the priors of the regression, bison_mice() for the imputed data, and extract_metric().

Examples

sim_data <- simulate_bison_model("binary", aggregated = TRUE)
df <- sim_data$df_sim
fit_edge <- bison_model(
  (event | effort) ~ dyad(node_1_id, node_2_id),
  data = df,
  model_type = "binary_conjugate",
  priors = get_default_priors("binary_conjugate")
)
# Does age difference predict edge weight? The multi-membership term accounts
# for edges that share a node not being independent.
fit_dyadic <- bison_brm(
  bison(edge_weight(node_1_id, node_2_id)) ~ age_diff + (1 | mm(node_1_id, node_2_id)),
  fit_edge,
  df,
  num_draws = 5 # Use more (e.g. 100) in a real analysis
)
